prompt: What does it mean to bake the shop's web server image?
hint: When does the installing happen?

choices.text: Installing nginx on each machine as it boots, from a script in its user data
choices.why: That is configuring at boot: the work is redone on every machine, every time.

choices.text: Doing the installation once, into an image, before any machine exists
choices.why: Yes. Every machine then starts as a copy and has nothing left to install.

choices.text: Running Ansible against every machine a minute after it starts
choices.why: Still configuration of a running machine, which is what baking removes.

choices.text: Caching the archive's packages on the laptop
choices.why: A cache speeds a download; the machine would still install at boot.

prompt: Three web servers configure themselves at boot with `apt-get install nginx`. They were started on day 1, day 9 and day 20. What can be said about the nginx they run?
hint: Whose version does each one get?

choices.text: The same version, because the command is the same
choices.why: The command is the same; the archive it reads is not, so each gets its own day's version.

choices.text: Whatever each boot day's archive offered
choices.why: Right, and no file records which, which is the difference baking removes.

choices.text: The version that was current when the plain image was built
choices.why: The plain image has no nginx at all; it is installed later, at boot.

choices.text: The newest one, since apt upgrades nginx on every reboot
choices.why: Nothing upgrades it after the install; each keeps what its boot got.

prompt: Which of these belongs in the baked image rather than being supplied at boot?
hint: Is it the same on every copy?

choices.text: The database password
choices.why: A secret in the image is a secret in every copy; it is read at boot from a secret store.

choices.text: The address of the production database
choices.why: It differs per environment, so it is given at boot.

choices.text: Which environment the machine belongs to
choices.why: That differs per copy, which is exactly what stays out of the image.

choices.text: nginx and its version
choices.why: Yes: packages are the same on every copy, so they are installed once, at build time.

prompt: On a sale day the shop starts twenty extra web servers at once, while the Ubuntu package mirror is overloaded. Which servers come up slowly or not at all?
hint: Which kind needs the mirror at the moment it starts?

choices.text: The ones started from a baked image
choices.why: A baked image already holds the packages; the mirror was needed at build time, days before.

choices.text: The ones that install their packages at boot
choices.why: Right: their start depends on the mirror answering at that moment, the busiest one.

choices.text: Both kinds equally, because every machine boots from an image
choices.why: Both boot from an image, but only one then downloads anything.

choices.text: Neither, because AWS keeps a copy of the mirror in each region
choices.why: The lesson's point holds whoever runs the mirror: a fried start needs it to answer.

prompt: Match each block of `web.pkr.hcl` to its job.
hint: Three top-level blocks and two kinds of block inside `build`.

pairs.right: Where the temporary machine comes from
A step run inside the temporary machine
Something done to the image after it is saved

prompt: Without `commit = true` in the `source` block, what would the Docker build leave behind?
hint: What turns the temporary container into something kept?

choices.text: An image tagged `shop-web:1.0.0` anyway
choices.why: There would be no image to tag; the commit is what makes one.

choices.text: No image at all, only a container that is thrown away
choices.why: Right. The provisioners would run in a container that is then thrown away, which is a run and not a build.

choices.text: A running container with nginx serving the page
choices.why: Packer kills the temporary container at the end either way.

choices.text: An AMI in moto
choices.why: The docker builder never talks to AWS; AMIs come from `amazon-ebs`.

prompt: Why does this lesson's template say `pull = false`?
hint: What happened when Packer asked Docker Hub while the lesson was recorded?

choices.text: Docker Hub refused pulls with `429 Too Many Requests`
choices.why: Yes, during the recording, so the build used the copy already on the machine. Leaving it out is the ordinary setting.

choices.text: Pulling is what makes the build reproducible
choices.why: The opposite: a pull of a tag can bring a different image. Pinning by digest is what makes it reproducible.

choices.text: The docker builder cannot pull images at all, so the setting is required
choices.why: It pulls by default; the lesson's first attempt was refused by the registry, not by Packer.

choices.text: It stops the image being pushed to Docker Hub after the build
choices.why: Pushing is a separate post-processor; `pull` is about the base image coming in.

prompt: To build the shop's image as an AMI on AWS instead of a Docker image, which part of the template changes most?
hint: Where does the temporary machine come from?

choices.text: The provisioner, which has to be rewritten for EC2
choices.why: The same shell steps run inside an EC2 instance as inside a container.

choices.text: The `build` block, which AWS does not support
choices.why: The build block is the same; it just names a different source.

choices.text: The `source` block, which names the builder and its settings
choices.why: Yes: `source "amazon-ebs"` with a region, an instance type and an `ami_name`.

choices.text: Nothing; Packer detects the target from the credentials
choices.why: The builder is named explicitly in the source block's first label.

prompt: Put what `packer build` did for the Docker image in order.
hint: The tag comes from a post-processor.
items: Run the provisioner's script inside it
Commit the container as an image
trap: Tagging before the commit is the usual slip: there is no image to tag until the container has been saved.

prompt: On the machine this lesson was recorded on, `packer build` finished successfully, yet `docker run shop-web:1.0.0` stopped at once. Why did Packer not notice?
hint: What does Packer check after each step?

choices.text: Packer ignores errors inside provisioners
choices.why: A provisioner step that fails stops the build; none failed here.

choices.text: It only checks each step's exit status
choices.why: Right. Installing nginx succeeded; starting it on a machine without IPv6 is a different question, answered only by running the image.

choices.text: The commit lost the nginx configuration written by apt
choices.why: The configuration was there; `grep` found its `listen` lines in the image.

choices.text: `packer validate` had already approved the template
choices.why: Validate checks the template's syntax; it never runs anything.

prompt: After fixing the template, why did Ana build `1.0.1` instead of building `1.0.0` again?
hint: What should a version name?

choices.text: Docker refuses to reuse a tag
choices.why: Docker would move the tag without complaint; that is the danger.

choices.text: `1.0.0` already names an image, and that image does not change
choices.why: Yes. A faulty version is followed by a newer one, never rebuilt under the old number.

choices.text: Packer increments the patch number on every build that follows a failure
choices.why: Packer invents no number; the template, and later a variable, gives it.

choices.text: Old images have to be deleted before a tag is used again
choices.why: Nothing has to be deleted; the point is not to reuse the number at all.

prompt: Before building, `packer ___ .` checks the template and builds nothing; it printed `The configuration is valid.`
hint: Terraform has a command of the same name.

prompt: What did `packer build .` do once `version` and `commit` were variables with no default?
hint: Neither was given on the command line.

choices.text: Built `shop-web:latest`
choices.why: Packer does not make a version up; it refused to start.

choices.text: Refused, with `Unset variable`
choices.why: Yes, once for each of the two, and nothing was built.

choices.text: Asked for the values interactively, as Terraform does
choices.why: It printed an error and stopped; there was no prompt.

choices.text: Reused `1.0.1`, the last version in the template
choices.why: The number was taken out of the template in that same diff.

prompt: Where can someone find which git commit built `shop-web:1.1.0`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two places were written by the build.

choices.text: In the image's `org.opencontainers.image.revision` label
choices.why: Yes; it travels inside the image, so a machine running it can be asked.

choices.text: In `manifest.json`, under `custom_data`
choices.why: Yes; that is what the next step of a pipeline reads.

choices.text: In the image's tag
choices.why: The tag carries the version only, `1.1.0`.

choices.text: In the `packer` block's `required_plugins`
choices.why: That block names plugins and their versions, not the template's commit.

choices.text: In the image id Docker printed
choices.why: The id is a hash of the image; it says nothing about git.

prompt: Two web servers were started from `shop-web:latest`, one on Monday and one on Friday, and nobody edited any file in between. Are they running the same image?
hint: What does a build in between do to `latest`?

choices.text: Yes, because the files that describe them did not change
choices.why: The files say `latest`, and `latest` can point at a different image on Friday.

choices.text: Not necessarily
choices.why: Right: any build in the week moves the tag, and nothing in the files records that it moved.

choices.text: Yes, because Docker refuses to start an image whose tag has moved
choices.why: Docker starts whatever the tag points at, without comment.

choices.text: No, never, because `latest` changes every hour
choices.why: It changes when somebody builds, which is the problem: you cannot tell from the name.

prompt: After the `1.1.0` build, how many images did `docker images shop-web` list?
hint: Count `1.0.0` too: nothing deleted it.

prompt: Ana changes `web_version` from `1.0.1` to `1.1.0` in `terraform.tfvars`. Why does the plan replace the instance instead of updating it?
hint: Look for the comment at the end of the `ami` line.

choices.text: Because the `Version` tag changed
choices.why: A tag alone is an update in place; the tag changes here only because the instance is replaced anyway.

choices.text: Because `create_before_destroy` forces every change to be a replacement
choices.why: It only sets the order of a replacement; it does not cause one.

choices.text: `ami` forces replacement
choices.why: Yes: a different image means a different instance, so the plan says `# forces replacement`.

choices.text: Because moto cannot update instances
choices.why: The plan is computed by the provider, the same against moto as against AWS.

prompt: The apply printed `Creating...` for the new instance before `Destroying...` for the old one. What made that the order?
hint: A lifecycle argument from lesson 6.

choices.text: `create_before_destroy = true` in the instance's `lifecycle` block
choices.why: Yes: `+/-`, create replacement and then destroy, with the old one kept as a deposed object meanwhile.

choices.text: Terraform always creates first when the image changes
choices.why: The default order is destroy first; lesson 6 showed the gap that leaves.

choices.text: The `data "aws_ami"` lookup ran before the instance
choices.why: The lookup decides which image, not the order of the replacement.

choices.text: The variable `web_version` has no default
choices.why: That forces a value to be given; it says nothing about ordering.

prompt: `1.1.0` turns out to be faulty. What does the lesson do to roll back?
hint: The same path as a rollout.

choices.text: Logs in to the instance and reinstalls the old nginx
choices.why: That edits a running machine, which this model never does.

choices.text: Runs `terraform destroy` and applies again from scratch
choices.why: Far more than needed; the change is one value.

choices.text: Rebuilds `1.1.0` with the old template
choices.why: That would give one number two images; the older version already exists.

choices.text: `git revert`, then a plan that replaces the instance again
choices.why: Yes: `1.0.1` is back in `terraform.tfvars`, and the instance is replaced towards the older image.

prompt: In the plan, the line for the image ends with `# forces ___`, which is why the instance is not updated in place.
hint: The word the plan also uses in `must be replaced`.

prompt: What does `ubuntu@sha256:…` guarantee that `ubuntu:24.04` does not?
hint: Can the name be moved to other contents?

choices.text: That the image was built recently, with this month's updates
choices.why: It guarantees the opposite kind of thing: the same contents, however old.

choices.text: That it names the same contents every time it is used
choices.why: Yes: the digest is a hash of the contents, so different contents would have a different name.

choices.text: That Canonical signed the image
choices.why: A digest identifies contents; it says nothing about who published them.

choices.text: That the pull will be faster because Docker skips the registry
choices.why: Speed is not the point; the template keeps `pull = false` for its own reason.

prompt: The template pins nginx to the exact update the archive offered on build day. A month later the archive has replaced that update with a newer one. What happens on the next build?
hint: The version table listed the release's version and the newest update.

choices.text: It fails at `apt-get install`, before any image is made
choices.why: Yes, loudly and on the day of the build, instead of quietly producing something different. Moving the pin is then a reviewed commit.

choices.text: apt installs the newer version without saying so
choices.why: That is what an unpinned install does; a pin asks for one exact version.

choices.text: Packer reuses the nginx from the previous image
choices.why: Each build starts from the base image; nothing is carried over from earlier builds.

choices.text: The build succeeds, because the digest pins the packages too
choices.why: The digest pins the base image; nginx is installed afterwards, from the archive.

prompt: A teammate says pinning the base digest and every package means the shop never gets security fixes. What does the lesson answer?
hint: Pins make updates deliberate.

choices.text: Pinned images are patched automatically by the registry
choices.why: Nothing patches an image after it is built; that would make it mutable.

choices.text: Security fixes go in at boot, through apt, on top of the baked image
choices.why: That brings back configuring at boot, and the drift and boot-time cost with it.

choices.text: A scheduled rebuild bumps the pins in a commit and ships a new version
choices.why: Right: updates arrive on a schedule as reviewed diffs, and an urgent fix takes the same path the same day.

choices.text: He is right, which is why the lesson pins only the base image
choices.why: The lesson pins both, and rebuilds to move them.

prompt: Somebody edited `index.html` inside the running container `shop-web-live`. What did `docker diff` show after the container was replaced from `shop-web:1.2.0`?
hint: The new container is the image again.

choices.text: The edited file, marked `C`
choices.why: That was before the replacement; the edit lived only in the old container.

choices.text: An error, because the container had been replaced
choices.why: The new container has the same name and diffs cleanly against its image.

choices.text: Nothing in the web directory
choices.why: Yes: the hand fix was lost, by design, and `curl` served the image's own page again.

choices.text: The edit, copied into the image by Docker
choices.why: Docker never writes a container's changes back into its image unless somebody commits it.

prompt: Which inputs did Ana pin to make the build reproducible? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two names that moved, plus what was already in git.

choices.text: The base image, by digest
choices.why: Yes, so the start is the same contents every time.

choices.text: nginx, by exact package version
choices.why: Yes, read from `apt-cache policy` on that same base.

choices.text: The template itself, by its git commit
choices.why: Yes; the commit is recorded in the label and the manifest.

choices.text: The image id, by writing it into the template
choices.why: The id is an output of the build, not an input; it cannot be known before.

choices.text: The time of the build, so timestamps match
choices.why: Timestamps still differ; reproducible here means the same software, not the same bytes.

prompt: A security update to nginx is published. Put the steps that get it into production in order.
hint: The image is built and checked before Terraform hears of it.
items: Commit the new nginx pin to the template
Build the next version with `packer build -var version=…`
Start the image and check that it answers
Change `web_version` in `terraform.tfvars` and review the plan
Apply, which creates the new instance before destroying the old
trap: Changing `terraform.tfvars` before the image exists is the usual slip: the lookup by name finds no image and the plan fails.

prompt: At 2 a.m. an engineer fixes a broken page by editing it inside the running web server, and the site recovers. What happens to the fix?
hint: Where does the next machine come from?

choices.text: It stays until somebody runs `terraform apply` with no changes
choices.why: An apply with no changes replaces nothing; the fix lasts exactly as long as that machine.

choices.text: It is lost at the next replacement, unless it goes into the template
choices.why: Right: a hand fix is drift, and under this model the next machine is the image again. It has to ship as a new version.

choices.text: Packer notices the drift and includes it in the next build
choices.why: Packer builds from the template and a base image; it never looks at running machines.

choices.text: Terraform reports it as drift on the next plan
choices.why: A file inside the machine is invisible to the cloud's API, as lesson 1 showed.

prompt: A team bakes images but lets every instance run `apt-get upgrade` at boot "to stay patched". Which property of the lesson's approach have they given up?
hint: Is the machine still exactly its image?

choices.text: Being able to tag images with a version
choices.why: They can still tag; the tag just no longer describes what runs.

choices.text: Using Terraform to replace instances
choices.why: Terraform can still replace them; each replacement just runs something different.

choices.text: Running nginx in a container
choices.why: Containers or not, the issue is what changes after start.

choices.text: Machines that are exactly their image
choices.why: Right: each boot now installs whatever that day offers, so the version no longer says what runs. Patches belong in a rebuild.
